records.question: How do the IMF, the World Bank bodies and the BIS fit together, and where does the Fed connect?
records.answer: Treasury speaks for the U.S. at the IMF and the five World Bank Group bodies (IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, ICSID); the Fed Board is the U.S. member of the BIS. The Fed touches them at 5 points: U.S. policy seat; depositary and fiscal agent; SDR certificate chain; IMF surveillance; BIS membership. None of these gives the IMF or the Bank a say in Fed policy, or the Fed a vote inside them. Treasury's October 14, 2026 statement is a U.S. position, not yet a rule change at any of the institutions.

records.question: Which payment rails are being rebuilt around Swift, or alongside it?
records.answer: The world record holds 35 dated payment-plumbing moves in 10 regions, January 6, 2025 to July 7, 2026: China's CIPS signing foreign banks, BRICS Pay targeted for a pilot, Africa's PAPSS, Indonesia's QRIS reaching Japan, Korea and China, Project Nexus, and the ECB's Pontes and Appia links. Swift's own shared ledger has four readings: announced September 29, 2025; 'controlled initial use preparing' on the Japan map (September 15, 2026); 'MVP ready; pilots pending', grade M4, on the UK map (September 14, 2026); and, newest, 17 listed banks and 6 bank-published bilateral pilot cases (October 19, 2026).

records.question: What can the U.S. block or decide in each international body, and what can't it?
records.answer: Across 27 bodies, U.S. power sits in five different places: a veto, consensus seat or blocking share in 5 (United Nations, NATO, International Monetary Fund, ITER, Board of Peace), money leverage in 8, domestic implementation in 8, command or facility access in 5 and agenda power in 6. A gate can stop specified action but does not give command: at the UN Security Council, procedural matters require nine votes and are not vetoable; affirmative action still needs nine votes.

records.question: What does the U.S. pay, and how does it vote, in each international body?
records.answer: The U.S. share runs from 49.99% (Organization of American States, 2026 assessed quota) down to 9.09% (ITER, construction sharing baseline). At the UN it pays 22% of the regular budget and 26.1371% of peacekeeping, but still has one Assembly vote. Paying more buys more votes only where votes are weighted by money, at the IMF and World Bank: the U.S. IMF share can block decisions requiring 85% of total voting power; IBRD influence derives from shareholding.

records.question: Which international bodies has the U.S. left, and when does each exit take effect?
records.answer: Saved evidence through October 4, 2026. The U.S. has completed withdrawal from 1 treaty regime: the Paris Agreement (effective January 27, 2026). Its exit from the World Health Organization is claimed effective January 22, 2026 but disputed: WHO still treated the U.S. as a member in arrears in May 2026. UNESCO exit takes effect December 31, 2026. The parent UN climate treaty (UNFCCC) exit takes effect February 27, 2027. On February 3, 2025 it stopped taking part in the UN Human Rights Council and cut its money to UNRWA, without leaving the UN. For 10 other bodies an exit clause exists but no U.S. notice was found.

records.question: How could the U.S. leave each international organization?
records.answer: Each of the 27 bodies has its own exit route. Where the founding text names a period, it runs from immediately (Board of Peace) and on receipt of notice (International Monetary Fund) to 90 days (Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons), six months (World Trade Organization, World Intellectual Property Organization), one year (NATO, OECD, International Civil Aviation Organization, International Maritime Organization, International Telecommunication Union) and two years (Organization of American States). For NATO the record adds: 'U.S. domestic statute requires Senate or Congress route'. 3 name a notice route without a period in the record (International Atomic Energy Agency, World Bank Group, ITER). 6 have no simple withdrawal clause (the United Nations Charter has none) and 4 are not memberships the U.S. could leave. 3 exits already carry a date: World Health Organization, UNESCO, Paris Agreement; the WHO exit, stated effective January 22, 2026, is disputed.

records.question: Is anything replacing the international bodies the U.S. is leaving?
records.answer: Not wholesale: the registry counts 0 wholesale replacements among the 27 bodies (as of October 4, 2026). 17 bodies still do their job with no successor. 4 were left, given notice to leave, or reduced participation in with no successor at all: UN Human Rights Council, UNRWA, UNESCO, Paris Agreement. Only 3 show a changed default route, each for one bounded job: U.S. foreign health aid now goes through the America First Global Health Strategy bilateral network (the WHO's universal functions are retained); WTO appeals for participating non-U.S. Members go through the MPIA; and a U.S. side-by-side tax regime sits inside the OECD. Two pieces of new machinery exist (Artemis Accords, Board of Peace), and Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science is doctrine only. The Board of Peace's Gaza field handoff was incomplete in September 2026. UNESCO remains under notice until December 31, 2026; pending departure is not effective exit.

records.question: How does a UN decision get made, paid for and carried out, and who controls each step?
records.answer: A General Assembly decision passes through 13 steps, each with its own controller: Member States authorize; a state, organ or the Secretary-General asks for an agenda item; the General Committee filters it; a Main Committee takes the work; sponsors and co-facilitators write the text; the Assembly adopts it (two thirds for budget and other important questions, a simple majority otherwise); then the Fifth Committee and ACABQ decide the money, the Secretary-General carries it out, and auditors and Member States review it. Adoption is not funding, and funding is not delivery.
